findings.who: A graduate whose mother paid the 2025 student loan interest as a gift, or whose employer or nonprofit internship paid it and added it to W-2 box 1. The graduate is legally obligated on the loan and no one claims them as a dependent.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you (or your spouse) paid interest'. Someone else made the payments, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33, Interest paid by others: 'If you are the person legally obligated to make interest payments and someone else makes a payment of interest on your behalf, you are treated as receiving the payments from the other person and, in turn, paying the interest.' Example 2: 'As a gift, your mother made this payment ... you can deduct this payment of interest.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was interest paid in 2025, by you or by anyone else (a parent, an employer, a program), on a student loan that you (or your spouse) are legally bound to repay?' Then use the existing assisted_any question to remove employer-plan, health-program and 529 payments.

findings.who: A borrower whose 2025 payments the lender applied only to principal, but whose loan carries capitalized interest or a loan origination fee. Form 1098-E box 2 may flag this.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the lender statement as principal only, so they believe they 'paid interest' of nothing.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33: the remaining capitalized interest is applied 'to the principal payments in the order in which they were made' and 'the remaining amount of principal of both payments is treated as interest for tax purposes'. The example allocates $5 of the loan origination fee to the principal portion of each monthly payment and treats it as interest.
findings.fix: Ask whether any payment was made on a student loan in 2025, including principal-only and voluntary payments. Add help: 'Payments of principal can count as interest if interest was added to the loan balance or the loan had an origination fee; see box 2 of Form 1098-E.'

findings.who: A parent repaying a federal Parent PLUS loan, or a private loan, taken out for a child who was their dependent. Also a filer with a bank personal loan used only for tuition, fees, room and board.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'student loan' as a loan for their own schooling, or as a loan labeled 'student loan'. A parent thinks 'the student loan is my child's'. A personal-loan borrower thinks 'I have a personal loan, not a student loan'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi pp. 98–99: 'A qualified student loan is any loan you took out to pay the qualified higher education expenses for any of the following individuals who were eligible students. 1. Yourself or your spouse. 2. Any person who was your dependent when the loan was taken out.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'Count any loan you or your spouse took out to pay college or vocational school costs for yourself, your spouse or a dependent. This includes Parent PLUS loans and bank or personal loans used only for those costs.'

findings.who: A borrower who paid less than $600 of interest in 2025, or who made voluntary payments during a forbearance or deferment, and received no Form 1098-E.
findings.why_no: The filer associates student loan interest with the 1098-E form, or with required payments, and answers no when no form arrived or no payment was due.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33, When Must Interest Be Paid?: 'You can deduct all interest you paid during the year on your student loan, including voluntary payments, until the loan is paid off.'
findings.fix: Move the existing help 'A lender may send no form for a small amount of interest' onto the gate. Add: 'Include voluntary payments made while payments were paused.'

findings.who: A filer whose employer runs a student loan repayment benefit that paid part of the filer's loan in 2025. The employer excluded the payments from Form W-2 box 1 as a section 127 educational assistance program, and the filer's Form 1098-E counts the interest those payments covered.
findings.why_no: The filer cannot tell whether the benefit is an 'educational assistance program'. They may think of it as a perk or as pay, not under that legal name, and answer no. They may also read Example 1 in p970 (employer-paid interest is deductible) as covering their case.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33: "For payments made after March 27, 2020, do not deduct as interest on a student loan any interest paid by your employer under an educational assistance program."
findings.fix: Ask a fact the filer can check: "Did your (or your spouse's) employer pay any of your student loan in 2025?" If yes, ask whether the payment was included in Form W-2 box 1 wages. Treat interest paid with excluded (not-in-box-1) employer payments as assisted.

findings.who: A physician or nurse in the NHSC Loan Repayment Program or a state health-professional loan repayment program. The program paid tax-free money to the filer, and the filer then paid the loan servicer, including interest.
findings.why_no: The money came to the filer ('repayments made to you'), and the filer paid the lender. The words 'any of the interest was paid ... through ... loan repayment assistance' suggest a third party paying the lender. The filer believes they paid the interest themselves and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 5: "Student loan repayments made to you are tax free if you received them for ... The National Health Service Corps (NHSC) Loan Repayment Program ... You can't deduct the interest you paid on a student loan to the extent payments were made through your participation in any of the above programs."
findings.fix: Ask: "Did you (or your spouse) receive money from, or have loan payments made by, the NHSC Loan Repayment Program or a state health-professional loan repayment program in 2025, whether paid to you or to your lender?" Then ask how much of the interest those funds covered.

findings.who: A recent graduate whose parent, as owner of a 529 plan, took a distribution and used it (or gave it to the graduate) to pay the graduate's student loan interest. Alternatively, a filer who took a 529 distribution sent to themselves and later paid the servicer with it.
findings.why_no: The filer cannot tell whether the earnings part of the distribution is 'tax-free qualified tuition program earnings'. That depends on the $10,000 lifetime limit and on the qualified-expense rules. The student may also not know the money came from a 529, since the parent made the payment. Because the distribution did not go straight to the lender, the filer may think the interest was not paid 'from' QTP earnings.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, line 21: "Don't include any amount paid from a distribution of earnings made from a qualified tuition program (QTP) after 2018 to the extent the earnings are treated as tax free because they were used to pay student loan interest."
findings.fix: Ask: "Was any student loan interest paid with money withdrawn from a 529 plan, by you, your spouse, or anyone else (for example a parent)?" If yes, find the tax-free earnings portion from Form 1099-Q and the student-loan limit, instead of asking the filer to classify it.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse's employer (or only the spouse's NHSC award) covered part of the spouse's student loan interest.
findings.why_no: The gated question 'How much of the interest was paid that way?' and the help may be read as about the primary filer's own loan. Only the parent helper says 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)'. The primary filer answers no about their own loan.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33: "do not deduct as interest on a student loan any interest paid by your employer under an educational assistance program" (applies to whichever spouse's loan interest is on the joint return).
findings.fix: Repeat 'you or your spouse' in the gate question and in the amount question: "Was any of your or your spouse's student loan interest paid ...?"

findings.who: A filer whose private lender sent a Form 1098-E for a loan whose disbursement exceeded tuition and housing. The school refunded the excess, which the filer spent on a car or living costs outside the program.
findings.why_no: The lender calls it a student loan and the 1098-E reports the interest, so the filer reads 'not a qualified student loan' as not applying. Nothing in the words says that spending any of the proceeds on other things disqualifies the whole loan.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'a loan isn’t a qualified student loan if (a) any of the proceeds were used for other purposes'
findings.fix: Ask about checkable facts before the label: 'Was any of the money from any of these loans used for something other than tuition, fees, room and board, books or supplies (including refunds of excess aid you kept)? Answer yes even if the lender calls it a student loan or sent Form 1098-E.'

findings.who: A filer who borrowed for a college program from a parent, grandparent or sibling, or from a relative who funded the loan with a 401(k) plan loan, and paid interest under a written note.
findings.why_no: The loan was taken out only to pay tuition, so the filer considers it a qualified student loan. 'Not a qualified student loan' gives no hint that the lender's identity, a related person or money borrowed under an employer plan, disqualifies it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'or (b) the loan was from either a related person or a person who borrowed the proceeds under a qualified employer plan or a contract purchased under such a plan'
findings.fix: Add a separate yes/no: 'Was any of the loans from a relative (parent, grandparent, child, sibling, spouse), from a business or trust you or they control, or funded by money the lender borrowed from a 401(k) or similar employer plan?' Count a yes toward the gate.

findings.who: A parent who took out a loan years ago for a child, grandchild, niece or partner's child who was not their dependent and could not have been claimed when the loan was made. Another case is a loan for a student not enrolled at least half-time in a degree program at an eligible institution.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'qualified' as 'used for school' and does not know the test is who the student was, and their status when the loan was taken out. The person may also be a dependent now, which seems to confirm qualification.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi pp. 98–99: 'any loan you took out to pay the qualified higher education expenses for any of the following individuals who were eligible students. 1. Yourself or your spouse. 2. Any person who was your dependent when the loan was taken out. 3. Any person you could have claimed as a dependent for the year the loan was taken out'
findings.fix: Ask whose education each loan paid for and their relationship to you when the loan was taken out (you, your spouse, your dependent then, someone else). Also ask whether the program was at an eligible college, university or vocational school. Classify from the answers.

findings.who: A filer paying 2025 interest on a loan taken out in an earlier year. At that time the borrower met the tests differently, or the proceeds were partly used for non-education costs.
findings.why_no: The question is asked in the context of '2025' interest, so the filer judges qualification by their situation today, not as of when the loan was taken out and the proceeds spent.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'Any person who was your dependent when the loan was taken out' / 'any of the proceeds were used for other purposes'
findings.fix: State in help text: 'Judge each loan by the facts when it was taken out and by how all of its proceeds were used, even if that was before 2025.'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly in which one spouse voluntarily paid interest on a sibling's or adult child's student loan. Neither spouse signed or co-signed that loan.
findings.why_no: The help ties 'legally obligated' to 'you' alone. The filer, who is not the paying spouse, answers about their own loans and answers no for the household.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33: 'Interest you paid on a loan if, under the terms of the loan, you aren’t legally obligated to make interest payments.'
findings.fix: Reword: 'Did you or your spouse pay interest on any loan that neither of you signed or co-signed (for example, a child's, sibling's or friend's student loan)?'

findings.who: A parent who makes payments on an adult child's federal or private student loan that is in the child's name only, believing that paying it makes them responsible for it.
findings.why_no: 'Legally obligated' is read as a moral or practical obligation ('I pay it every month'), not as being a borrower or co-signer under the loan's terms.
findings.irs_text: p970 p. 33: 'Interest you paid on a loan if, under the terms of the loan, you aren’t legally obligated to make interest payments.'
findings.fix: Ask the checkable fact: 'Is your (or your spouse's) name on each loan as borrower or co-signer?' Treat any no as interest you were not legally obligated to pay.
